problems.title: Two Sum
problems.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target. You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. You can return the answer in any order.
problems.input_format: First line contains space-separated integers for nums, second line contains target integer.

hints.conceptual: A brute force approach checks every pair (O(n^2)). Can you check if the complement (target - current_number) has already been seen in O(1) time?
hints.algorithm: Iterate through the array while maintaining a Hash Map (dictionary) mapping value -> index. For each element num, compute complement = target - num.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.description: Given a string s containing just the characters "(", ")", "{", "}", "[" and "]", determine if the input string is valid. An input string is valid if open brackets are closed by the same type of brackets and in the correct order.
problems.input_format: A string s containing bracket characters.

hints.conceptual: Parentheses must follow Last-In, First-Out order. What fundamental data structure embodies LIFO?
hints.algorithm: Use a Stack. Push opening brackets onto the stack. When encountering a closing bracket, check if it matches the stack top element, then pop.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the reversed list. Can you solve it both iteratively and recursively in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is the range [0, 5000].

starter_code.python:
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
def reverseList(head):
    # Write solution here
    pass

hints.conceptual: To reverse a direction of pointer A -> B, you need to point B -> A. What happens to the rest of the list when you break the link?
hints.algorithm: Maintain three pointers: prev (initially None), curr (initially head), and next_node (temporary storage before updating curr.next).
hints.pseudocode:
prev = None
curr = head
while curr is not None:
    next_temp = curr.next
    curr.next = prev
    prev = curr
    curr = next_temp
return prev
hints.solution:
def reverseList(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        next_node = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = next_node
    return prev

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.description: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. A substring is a contiguous non-empty sequence of characters within a string.
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.

examples.explanation: The answer is "abc", with the length of 3.
The answer is "b", with the length of 1.
The answer is "wke", with length 3 ("pwke" is a subsequence, not substring).

hints.conceptual: Think of a dynamic sliding window [left, right] that expands until a duplicate is found, then contracts.
hints.algorithm: Use a Hash Map storing char -> last_seen_index. When char at right index is already inside current window (index >= left), advance left to last_seen_index + 1.

problems.title: Course Schedule (Cycle Detection & TopoSort)
problems.description: There are a total of numCourses courses you have to take, labeled from 0 to numCourses - 1. You are given an array prerequisites where prerequisites[i] = [a_i, b_i] indicates that you must take course b_i first if you want to take course a_i. Return true if you can finish all courses. Otherwise, return false.
constraints: All the pairs prerequisites[i] are unique.

examples.explanation: There are a total of 2 courses. To take course 1 you should have finished course 0. So it is possible.
Course 1 requires 0 and course 0 requires 1. Circular dependency makes it impossible.

hints.conceptual: Courses and prerequisites form a directed graph. Can you finish all courses if there is a directed cycle in the graph?
hints.algorithm: Kahn algorithm for Topological Sorting: Track in-degrees of all nodes. Enqueue all nodes with in-degree 0. As you process nodes, decrement neighbors in-degrees. If processed_count == numCourses, no cycle exists.

problems.title: Coin Change (Optimal Substructure DP)
problems.description: You are given an integer array coins representing coins of different denominations and an integer amount representing a total amount of money. Return the fewest number of coins that you need to make up that amount. If that amount of money cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return -1. You may assume you have an infinite number of each kind of coin.

hints.conceptual: Greedy choice (taking the largest coin first) does not always work! Example: coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6. Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins), but optimal is 3 + 3 (2 coins).
hints.algorithm: Define dp[i] as the minimum coins needed to make amount i. Base case: dp[0] = 0, all other dp[i] initialized to infinity. Transition: dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - c] + 1) for all coins c <= i.

problems.title: SQL: Second Highest Salary & Dense Ranking
problems.description: Write an SQL query to report the second highest salary from the Employee table. If there is no second highest salary, the query should report null.
constraints: id is the primary key column for this table.

hints.conceptual: Be careful of duplicate salaries! If two employees share the top salary, the next distinct salary is the second highest.
hints.algorithm: Use MAX(salary) WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee) or use DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC).
hints.pseudocode: SELECT MAX(salary) AS SecondHighestSalary FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);

posters.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in Production
posters.tagline: Grounded enterprise intelligence without costly fine-tuning or stale LLM hallucinations.
posters.definition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an architectural pattern that enhances large language model outputs by dynamically retrieving relevant, verifiable context from private enterprise document stores prior to generating responses.

how_it_works.title: Document Ingestion & Chunking
how_it_works.detail: Source documentation (PDFs, Confluence, API specs) is broken into semantic chunks with token overlap to maintain cross-boundary context.

how_it_works.title: Vector Embedding Generation
how_it_works.detail: Dense mathematical embedding representations (e.g. 768 or 1536 dimensions) are generated using specialized embedding models.

how_it_works.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) Retrieval
how_it_works.detail: At query time, student or user prompt is embedded, and HNSW index retrieves top-K semantically closest chunks via cosine distance.

how_it_works.title: Context Augmentation & Grounded Prompting
how_it_works.detail: The retrieved chunks are injected into the system prompt with strict provenance constraints, prompting the LLM to cite sources.

real_world_applications: Customer support deflection with enterprise internal knowledge bases
Healthcare clinical guideline assistants citing published medical journals
Financial regulatory compliance search over thousands of SEC filings
Campus placement and coding assistants providing verified syntax documentation

posters.title: Vector Databases & HNSW Indexing
posters.tagline: How Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs make million-vector similarity search run in sub-millisecond speeds.
posters.definition: Vector databases are specialized storage engines designed to store, index, and query high-dimensional vector embeddings efficiently using Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search algorithms.

how_it_works.title: Multi-layer Skip List Topology
how_it_works.detail: HNSW builds hierarchical graph layers where top layers have sparse long-range highway edges and bottom layers have dense local clusters.

how_it_works.title: Greedy Routing Algorithm
how_it_works.detail: Search begins at the topmost layer finding local minima, then drops down layer by layer refining closest candidates.

how_it_works.title: Distance Metrics Computation
how_it_works.detail: Calculates Cosine Similarity, Dot Product, or Euclidean (L2) distance using SIMD CPU instructions or GPU vector registers.

how_it_works.title: Filtered Hybrid Search
how_it_works.detail: Applies boolean metadata filtering (e.g., user_id, date, role) concurrently with vector distance traversal.

real_world_applications: Visual reverse image search across e-commerce product catalogs
Spotify personalized music playlist recommendations based on audio embeddings
Fraud detection through behavioral pattern vector clustering

practical_example.title: Cosine Similarity vs Euclidean Distance in Vector Space
practical_example.code_or_query:
import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(v1: np.ndarray, v2: np.ndarray) -> float:
    # Measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors (directional alignment)
    dot_product = np.dot(v1, v2)
    norm_v1 = np.linalg.norm(v1)
    norm_v2 = np.linalg.norm(v2)
    return dot_product / (norm_v1 * norm_v2)

# Normalizing vectors makes dot product equivalent to cosine similarity!
vec_a = np.array([0.2, 0.8, -0.5])
vec_b = np.array([0.1, 0.9, -0.4])
print(f"Similarity: {cosine_similarity(vec_a, vec_b):.4f}")
practical_example.explanation: In NLP and recommendation systems, vector length often reflects text length or frequency rather than semantic meaning; hence cosine similarity (orientation) is preferred over Euclidean distance.

posters.title: Apache Kafka: High-Throughput Distributed Event Log
posters.tagline: Decoupling distributed microservices with sequential disk I/O and zero-copy data transfer.
posters.definition: Apache Kafka is a distributed event store and stream processing platform that models all data streams as immutable, partitioned append-only commit logs.

how_it_works.title: Append-Only Commit Logs
how_it_works.detail: Messages are appended to the end of partition logs sequentially. Sequential disk writes are nearly as fast as random RAM access.

how_it_works.title: Partitioning & Consumer Groups
how_it_works.detail: Topics are partitioned across cluster brokers, enabling horizontal read/write scale across multiple consumers in a group.

how_it_works.title: Zero-Copy OS Transfer (sendfile)
how_it_works.detail: Kafka leverages the Linux OS sendfile syscall to stream data directly from OS page cache to network sockets without JVM memory copies.

how_it_works.title: Offset Tracking
how_it_works.detail: Consumers record their own progress via committed offsets in an internal __consumer_offsets topic, allowing message replaying.

real_world_applications: Financial transaction audit logs and real-time fraud alerts
Ride-sharing driver GPS telemetry location ingestion at 1M events/sec
Change Data Capture (CDC) syncing relational databases to search indexes

practical_example.title: Idempotent Kafka Consumer Pattern
practical_example.code_or_query:
def process_placement_event(event: dict, processed_cache: set) -> None:
    event_id = event.get("event_id")
    # Idempotency guard: prevent duplicate processing in at-least-once delivery
    if event_id in processed_cache:
        print(f"Duplicate event {event_id} ignored.")
        return

    # Execute critical business logic
    update_student_streak(event["student_id"])
    processed_cache.add(event_id)
practical_example.explanation: Because Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default, consumers must implement idempotent logic (deduplication keys) to prevent duplicate side-effects during network retries.

quizzes.question: Why is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) generally preferred over continual model fine-tuning for frequently updated internal technical documentation?
options: RAG eliminates the need to run any LLM inference compute.
RAG decouples knowledge updates from model retraining, allowing near-instant updates with verifiable source citations.
Fine-tuning completely prevents hallucinations whereas RAG does not.
RAG only works with open-source models while fine-tuning is proprietary.
quizzes.explanation_correct: Correct! Fine-tuning embeds static weights requiring hours or days of compute, whereas RAG updates happen instantly by updating the vector index and passing retrieved passages in the prompt.
explanation_distractors: Incorrect: RAG still requires LLM inference compute to synthesize the prompt and retrieved documents.
Incorrect: Fine-tuning does not guarantee zero hallucinations and often causes model drift or catastrophic forgetting.
Incorrect: RAG works with both proprietary API models (Gemini, Claude) and open-weights models (Llama).

quizzes.question: What is the primary trade-off when selecting chunk size during document embedding in a RAG pipeline?
options: Larger chunks provide more context to the LLM but dilute semantic specificity and consume more context window tokens.
Smaller chunks always produce better answers regardless of the topic.
Chunk size has no mathematical effect on vector embeddings.
Chunk sizes must be exact powers of 2 (e.g. 256, 512, 1024) or vector databases will reject them.
quizzes.explanation_correct: Correct! Large chunks capture broader paragraphs but might dilute the similarity vector; small chunks produce razor-sharp vector matches but may lose broader surrounding context.
explanation_distractors: Incorrect: Excessively small chunks (e.g., single sentences) lack context and can cause fragmented, confusing responses.
Incorrect: Vector embedding distance changes significantly depending on the chunked text.
Incorrect: Chunk sizes are measured in characters or tokens and do not have strict power-of-2 constraints.

quizzes.question: In production RAG systems, what technique is commonly applied immediately AFTER vector retrieval and BEFORE sending context to the LLM?
options: Dropping all retrieved chunks that have vowels.
Re-ranking with a Cross-Encoder model to re-score candidate relevance.
Converting all text into hexadecimal format.
Re-training the foundation model weights.
quizzes.explanation_correct: Correct! Bi-encoder vector search retrieves candidates in milliseconds, and a cross-encoder re-ranker accurately scores the top 20-50 candidates to send the top 3-5 to the LLM.
explanation_distractors: Incorrect: Dropping vowels destroys textual semantics.
Incorrect: Hexadecimal format increases token count drastically with zero benefit.
Incorrect: Re-training weights during the request lifecycle is impossible for real-time retrieval.

quizzes.question: What is the key advantage of HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) over Flat Indexing in vector similarity search?
options: Flat indexing is logarithmic O(log N) while HNSW is exponential.
Flat indexing calculates distance against every vector (O(N)), while HNSW approximates nearest neighbors in O(log N) through graph layers.
HNSW uses zero memory storage.
HNSW produces 100% mathematically exact nearest neighbors every time.
quizzes.explanation_correct: Correct! Flat indexing evaluates distance against all N vectors (exact but slow for large datasets). HNSW provides Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search with sub-millisecond logarithmic complexity.
explanation_distractors: Incorrect: Flat indexing is O(N) linear scan, not logarithmic.
Incorrect: HNSW requires additional memory to store multi-layer graph edge pointers.
Incorrect: HNSW is an ANN (approximate) algorithm with very high recall (e.g., 95-99%), not guaranteed 100% exact.

quizzes.question: Why are consumers in Apache Kafka designed to be responsible for tracking their own offsets?
options: Because Kafka brokers do not have disks.
It keeps the broker stateless with respect to consumer read positions, maximizing broker throughput and enabling consumers to replay past data.
Consumers must store offsets to encrypt messages.
Kafka only supports a single consumer per topic.
quizzes.explanation_correct: Correct! Removing consumer state tracking from broker memory simplifies broker design and allows consumers to easily rewind offsets to re-process historical events.
explanation_distractors: Incorrect: Kafka brokers persist all partition data to disk sequentially.
Incorrect: Offset tracking is about position metadata, not payload encryption.
Incorrect: Kafka supports multiple consumer groups reading independently from the same topic.

scenarios.sample_prompt: How would you systematically triage this issue? How will you determine whether this is an actual business downturn, an Airflow pipeline failure, a timezone offset bug, or currency conversion discrepancy, and how will you communicate with leadership?

evaluation_rubric.problem_clarification: Clarifies when the discrepancy began and checks pipeline execution statuses before making business assumptions.
evaluation_rubric.assumptions: Considers timezone boundary differences (UTC vs Local), pending transactions, or failed DAG runs in Airflow.

evaluation_rubric.alternatives_and_tradeoffs: Discusses temporary rollback vs urgent hotfix and automated alerting mechanisms for future pipeline health.
evaluation_rubric.communication: Maintains composure, provides clear executive summary with root cause and next steps without blaming teams.

scenarios.sample_prompt: How would you evaluate whether this surge is caused by covariate shift, concept drift, or upstream data pipeline corruption? What steps will you take to detect, isolate, and safely deploy an updated model?

evaluation_rubric.problem_clarification: Distinguishes between input data distribution shift P(X) and conditional probability change P(Y|X).
evaluation_rubric.assumptions: Identifies external macroeconomic variables and potential latency in ground truth label availability.
evaluation_rubric.technical_correctness: Proposes statistical drift metrics (Population Stability Index - PSI, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Wasserstein distance) and SHAP feature importance shifts.
evaluation_rubric.evidence_and_depth: Details shadow/canary model deployment, automated rollback thresholds, and retraining frequency with sample weighting.
evaluation_rubric.alternatives_and_tradeoffs: Discusses conservative threshold tightening vs aggressive retraining with sparse recent data.
evaluation_rubric.communication: Explains technical statistical concepts in business impact terms.
